The Verse on the Contemplation of Food by the Zen Master of Nanyue states: "The color and fragrance of this food are like the sandalwood wind, universally perfuming the worlds of the ten directions at once.
Sentient beings, whether ordinary or sagely, who have a karmic affinity will each receive its supreme flavor; those in the six realms who smell its fragrance will give rise to the bodhicitta.
One can produce the six pāramitās and the three practices through food. Please examine this contemplation carefully; why wait to harbor doubts?
Furthermore, the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states: "One should offer a single meal to all beings as an offering to the Buddhas and the assembly of worthy sages, and only then may one eat.
Is this not the contemplation of food? Question: Since the transformation of food relies on the power of mantras, what is the use of contemplation?

Answer: Contemplation supports the mantra, further enhancing its efficacy. Moreover, the mantra is the power of another (he-power), whereas contemplation is one's own power (self-power); yet, if there is only the mantra and no contemplation, [the benefit is incomplete].

For example, it is like a blind person who has others prepare a great assembly for giving; though they trust the words of others saying whether food has been obtained or not, they never see it for themselves.
If one adds visualization, it is like a person with sight who has others prepare a great assembly for giving and sees every detail with their own eyes, not relying on the words of others.
As the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* says regarding the instruction to visualize as if seeing with one's own eyes: [the text continues].
If a bodhisattva dwells upon dharmas while practicing giving, it is like a person entering darkness who sees nothing;
if one practices giving without dwelling upon dharmas, it is like a person with eyes seeing various forms when the light of the sun shines.
Now, to practice without contemplation is merely to act like a person entering darkness; to contemplate that there is no dwelling in accordance with the dharma-realm is precisely this.
The merit of practicing giving without abiding is, for example, like the empty space of the ten directions, inconceivable and immeasurable.
If one can practice contemplation when performing any Buddha-work, even down to offering a single flower or a single incense stick, one will not be obstructed by birth and death;

rather, every single instance will flow into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge). That even a small amount of precept-keeping or a small amount of giving leads to the fruit of Buddhahood is precisely due to this.

I hope that those who believe will linger over them, reading carefully and reflecting deeply; for when one fears greatly the karmic results manifest in this life and the retributions of the future—such as copper, iron, fire, and boiling water—is it not difficult to endure?
Homage to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, the ocean of the Greatly Compassionate Triple Gem. Now, desiring to follow the teachings and universally exhort all sentient beings, I say:
do not kill, do not eat meat. Together cultivate acts of kindness and compassion;
remain free from illness and preserve a long life. In the future, you shall attain the path of Buddhahood, as do all Buddhas and great Bodhisattvas.
Constantly for the sake of saving sentient beings, He sacrificed his head, eyes, body, and life— Countless as the sands of the Ganges.
He gave up his royal body to save a dove, Sacrificed his dragon life for the sake of ants, And provided flowing water to rescue the parched fish.
As a *sattva*, he satisfied a starving tiger; Throughout kalpas, he practiced compassion universally, And through the power of that compassionate goodness, he attained perfection.
The Buddha has no ordinary mind; only a mind of compassion remains.
If there are those who practice compassion—refraining from killing and not eating meat— I pray that the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power May always provide protection throughout every lifetime.
What the Buddha has taught regarding the taking of life: To kill is to kill one's own father and mother, And likewise to kill one's own wife and daughters.
Brothers and sisters, and all men and women included— All have once been our parents;
in birth after birth, we have received their wombs, From whom we inherited our physical forms.
The bodies of a single species of animal, with their bones and blood as vast as mountains and seas, In each and every class of being, the births are beyond calculation.
Wandering through the six realms of saṃsāra, we have repeatedly been relatives to one another;
therefore, eating various sentient beings is called eating the flesh of one's own parents.
Furthermore, contemplate that all bodies—whether my own flesh or the flesh of others—are in reality but a single flesh, like those living in front of and behind a house.
It is also called my own house; you should know that those who eat meat are eating their own flesh.
The Buddha contemplates the *tathāgatagarbha*—the realm of the Buddhas and the realm of sentient beings—as a single realm without a second realm;
all flesh is one flesh. Like an actor’s temporary transformation, it was originally the body of a single person.
If one wishes to kill a sentient being, one should conceive of them as a Buddha.
When hunters, butchers, and those who catch fish or birds are seen from afar by sentient beings, they all give rise to the fear of certain death, thinking:
"This person of evil mind, driven by greed for profit and the taste of meat, holds a sharp knife or arrow in hand."
Thinking of killing my body, whether by flying, diving, or hiding, they are filled with terror and flee far away.
They constantly harbor thoughts of great enmity toward all sentient beings; there is no difference between humans, animals, or anyone else who cherishes their own life and body.
If you wish to eat sentient beings, first try cutting the flesh from your own body.
Death is the ultimate suffering; who could not fear it? Yet you merely look at your own body and ask, "How can I eat the flesh of others?
To profit from killing sentient beings, you use wealth as a net to obtain various meats;
both parties incur the karma of killing. Upon death, you will fall into the Raurava Hell. Listen now, you who take life!
Upon death, one falls into the place of hell: An iron city eight thousand *yojanas* high, And likewise four thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth;
Filled with fierce, blazing flames, Its interior and exterior are glowing crimson.
Copper dogs guard its four gates, And the hell-wardens’ voices thunder like a storm, Their two eyes flashing like lightning.
Driven forth, you who take life shall enter therein to undergo suffering. A powerful being grasps an iron spear;
the spear is ten feet long, its sharp blade eight inches wide. It strikes the chest of the sinner, piercing through the breast and exiting from the back.
The agony is unbearable to hear, lasting for thousands of myriads of koṭis of years.
Undergoing such extreme suffering—listen now, you who eat meat!

After death, you shall fall into the Avīci Hell, where the iron house is both high and vast, measuring eighty thousand yojanas. Its four gates blaze with fierce flames that penetrate each other from north to south;
there are iron walls and iron lattices, and iron collars and shackles.
Each and every one is burned by fire, Causing them all to glow a deep crimson.
Eating flesh, they undergo this suffering for hundreds, thousands, ten millions, and billions of years. Listen, you who cook meat:
You shall fall into the Hell of Boiling Cauldrons, Which measures twelve thousand yojanas in depth and breadth, Where fierce fires blaze day and night.
The boiling water constantly seethes, and therein one undergoes great suffering.
Listen, you who were once a man roasting meat: for seventeen thousand years you shall fall into the Hell of the Hot Iron Bed.
That hell measures eight thousand yojanas in length and breadth; fierce fires burn beneath the bed, and the sinner lies upon it.
The heart, liver, and flesh are scorched and rotten for twelve thousand years. Listen, you who cut meat:
when one dies, they fall into the Chakua (Chopping and Carving) Hell. Five hundred powerful giants use sharp blades to sever the sinner into ten thousand pieces until they are reduced to fine dust.
Blown by the winds of karma, they return to life; thus it ends and begins again.
For twelve thousand years, you shall listen as you tend to a flock of chickens for one who craves their fatty flesh.
For a single chicken in a single day, five hundred insects are consumed;
the owner shall incur half the guilt and fall into hell together with the chicken. That hell is filled with scorching excrement, measuring eighty thousand *yojanas* in extent.
Humans and chickens alike enter therein, To remain for five hundred million years. Listen, you hunters!
You set snares and traps, Place nets and lay pitfall snares;
With sharp blades and released hawks and dogs, You surround and close in from all four sides, Pursuing and killing living beings, Who die and fall into the Iron Ax Hell.
Ten thousand spikes on every inch of the body; driven upward, they revolve once around the torso.
With ten thousand spikes piercing the entire frame, the whole body is completely permeated by them. The agony is unbearable;
for hundreds of thousands of millions of years, one undergoes this retributive suffering. Those who kill living beings and eat their flesh shall emerge from these various hells.
Taking on the bodies of hungry *rākṣasas*, lions, jackals, tigers, and wolves, As well as cats, wildcats, owls, hawks, and vultures, they seek only fresh flesh and blood.
Sentient beings each hide and protect [their own], not allowing them to find an opportunity;
Yet the fire of hunger constantly burns their hearts, and moment by moment they think of the meat of others. It is due to this evil habitual conditioning (*vāsanā*).
Those of great compassion have forever severed [this craving];
even if they should be born among humans, they will be crippled, short-lived, foolish, and slanderers of cause and effect. Upon death, they fall back into hell.
When the Buddha spoke these words, immeasurable rākṣasas wailed with grief and vowed to abstain from meat, as well as to protect those who abstain from meat.
Now that you have heard this sutra, why do you not reform your ways? To labor in vain as a human being is worse than being a hungry ghost.
Be careful not to burn mountains or wilds; be careful not to breach dikes or ponds;
do not cut down trees with nests in them; do not burn firewood harboring insects. If you see living beings being killed, [protect them].
Skillful means ever protect and deliver; Homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions!
O World-Honored One of Great Wisdom and Virtue, I wish to exhort sentient beings To renounce alcohol and seek clear wisdom.
As the Buddha has taught, drinking alcohol brings many faults and afflictions: Eighty thousand gates of worldly toil, And thirty-five kinds of loss.
All this has alcohol as its root; you all should observe this clearly. When one is intoxicated with wine, the mind becomes dazed and confused, and the six consciousnesses fall into total delusion.
Rulers and ministers lose their sense of restraint, fathers and sons sever the bonds of honor and subordination, and mothers and daughters throw the social order into chaos.
Ritual propriety can no longer restrain them, just as in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
There was Aṅgulimāla, who, intoxicated by wine, committed adultery with his mother;
having killed his father out of passion and then consorted with another woman, he took up a knife and likewise harmed her.
He was also like the great arhat Śāgata, who, while traveling through the country of Cetiya, gradually arrived at the village of Bhadda.
There was a great venomous dragon named Āmrapālī; that dragon was extremely fierce and malicious, causing harm to the villagers.

Once the Arhat had subdued the venomous dragon through his supernormal powers, the villagers, wishing to repay his kindness, prepared much milk-rice mixed with ghee. A woman, having prepared the rice-milk, [offered it].
Fearing he might contract a cold ailment, he took some colored wine and offered it to a great Arhat.
The Arhat, thinking this was water, drank it; the power of the wine then took effect, and he became so intoxicated that he fell at the temple gate, leaving his robes and bowl in another place.
When he regained consciousness, he employed his supernatural powers and was able to subdue a great venomous dragon.
After becoming intoxicated, one is like a dead person; unable even to subdue a frog.
The World-Honored One commanded the Arhats and the assembly of bhikṣus to go to the abode of those Arhats; it was for this reason that the precept against alcohol was established.
As the *Saddharma-smṛty-upasthāna Sūtra* says: "Yama reprimands and places the person [there], driving them into hell."
First, these verses were spoken: "Alcohol can disturb the human mind, Causing one to be like a sheep or other beast, unaware of what should or should not be done.
Thus, one should abandon alcohol. If a person is intoxicated by alcohol, they are no different from one who is dead.
If you wish to remain forever undying, That person should abandon alcohol."
Alcohol is the source of all faults; it can never bring benefit. It is a stairway to all evil realms and a place of darkness.
By drinking alcohol, one goes to hell and also reaches the realm of hungry ghosts;
one performs the karma of an animal, deceived by the fault of this liquor. Alcohol is the most poisonous among poisons.
It is the hell within hells, the greatest of all diseases—thus has the Buddha taught:
If a person drinks alcohol, they will rejoice without cause, become angry without cause, and commit evil without cause;
they will give rise to delusion toward the Buddha and ruin both worldly and world-transcending matters.
The fire of liberation burns away that which is called the single dharma of liquor.
If a person can renounce liquor and practice the true conduct of the Dharma and precepts, they will reach the supreme state, the place where there is neither death nor birth.
Do not drink the wine of ignorance, for it is the cause of manifold sufferings. The Śrāvakas abide in the liberation of clear knowledge.

It is like a person returning home intoxicated; when there is suffering from illness, one should contemplate that the root of disease arises from ignorance and craving. Habitual karma invites the fruit of sickness;
even Jīvaka, with all his medical arts, cannot cure it. How could worldly medicines or wine ever heal my ailment?
Alcohol is the root of heedlessness; by not drinking, one closes off the evil paths.
It would be better to sacrifice hundreds of thousands of bodies than to violate the precept against alcohol. It would be better for the body to wither away than to ever drink this wine.
Even if one were to violate the precepts and live for a full hundred years, it would not equal the merit of guarding the prohibitive precepts.
Immediately his body was relieved and he was certainly able to recover.
Thinking, "I still would not drink [the medicine], how much less now when I do not know for certain whether I will recover or not," he formed this resolute mind and felt great joy in his heart.
He immediately attained the vision of the Truth, and his ailment was instantly eliminated.
Listen, you who brew wine: upon death you shall fall into the Hell of Saline Dregs;
you shall also fall into boiling ashes for eighteen thousand years. Listen, you who sell clear liquor:
upon death you shall fall into the Hell of the Wine Pond, filled with molten copper; entering therein, you shall undergo suffering. Listen, you who drink wine!
Upon death, you shall fall into the Hell of Pouring Molten Copper; with your own hands, you shall pour the molten bronze into your mouth, drenching it day and night.
Listen well: if one takes wine and forcibly urges a person who observes the precepts to drink, after death they shall enter the Hell of the Ice Pond.
For eighty million years they shall suffer, their skin and flesh all torn asunder, dying and being reborn a hundred times each day and night.
Thereafter, for five hundred births, you were born without both arms. Listen:
whether by force or even in jest, if one gives wine to monks or nuns and compels them to drink it, they shall fall into the Hell of Severed Knees after death;
there, amidst six million years, they will become five hundred powerful giants.
His two knees were constantly severed; even for passing a wine vessel, he was without hands for five hundred lifetimes.
He constantly took the form of ants and lice, of worms, maggots, flies, and gnats.
For each of these ignorant and deluded insects, he remained for five hundred lifetimes. Listen, Gīta-pa: you sold wine and your comb fell into the well.
The Arhats drank its water, and eighty thousand sages became intoxicated.
Because of this, they vexed the holy ones and died, falling into the Hell of the Saw-Platform. For eighty thousand great kalpas, they constantly suffered the agony of being sawn apart.
Afterward, they emerged and attained human form; their bodies were three feet tall, and their complexions were a dark, bluish-black.
The ears and nostrils are blocked; there are no eyes, and the lips are shriveled and drawn back.

The hands and feet lack ten fingers—how much more so for a mind that breaks the precepts! Compelling others to drink wine, one frequently sees such foolish people of the world forcing others to eat meat and drink wine.
Being unable to purify oneself, they possess a total lack of shame.
Furthermore, by consuming impure food and by coercing others to break their precepts, one commits a grave offense.
It would be better to take a person’s life than to destroy another’s wholesome mind. Taking a life results in death and rebirth, though it does not necessarily lead to the three evil realms;
yet breaking the precepts causes one to lose the states of humans and devas, as well as the Dharma of liberation. Listen now as I renounce alcohol and meat.
The merit and benefit obtained thereby— were someone to take the seven treasures, a kingdom, a city, wife, and children and give them as alms,
it would not equal even a ten-millionth part of abstaining from alcohol and meat.
Even filling the great trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and giving them as alms is not equal to a ten-millionth part of abstaining from alcohol and meat.
Even if, for the sake of seeking merit, one were to smelt gold to fashion human figures numbering in the hundreds,
thousands, and tens of thousands, and offer them as extensive alms— this would not equal even a ten-millionth part of the merit of abstaining from wine and meat.
Furthermore, if there were a son of the Buddha who fashioned banners, flowers, and jeweled canopies, filling the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system...
To offer such things to the Buddha is not as good as abstaining from alcohol and meat.
The sin of transgression is grave, yet the merit of maintaining [the precepts] is profound. Good and evil manifest in long succession;
suffering and joy follow one another constantly. While you are still capable, quickly turn back; deliberate early on so that each may reform the heart.
Do not wait for impermanence to arrive; Like a jar filled with water, it sinks by itself. Exert yourselves and strive diligently together;
Await the grove of the seven treasures. This verse appears in various sutras. Those who read or recite it must always protect it; if one treats it with disrespect, it is [as if]... [the text ends].
The transgression incurred by showing contempt for the Mahāyāna sūtras and other scriptures is no small matter.

Regarding the chapter on the admonition against the five pungent vegetables, this was prompted by my recent illness; while sitting in quiet contemplation, I reflected that among the monastics and laity today, many violate the Buddha’s prohibitions for reasons that are not urgent.
This refers to the five pungent vegetables (*pañca-garaka*), which are detrimental to the stomach and mouth; to eat them without cause is a vain obstacle to the Way and results in profound suffering.
He then investigated their origins to demonstrate them to his later followers. As for the "five pungents": first, garlic; second, leeks;

third, scallions; fourth, shallots; and fifth, *xingju* (which is *xianqiu*, or raw onion). The Tripiṭaka Master Cimin remarked that this land lacks the fifth pungent vegetable, having personally tasted it [in India].
In the kingdom of Khotan, I saw its roots; they resemble turnips in shape and have an odor like garlic.

They are falsely called *yuntai* (coriander) and *yunsui* (cumin), but these are not among the category of pungent vegetables. The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states: "If you, O sons of the Buddha, you must not eat the five pungent roots:
garlic, leeks, scallions, onions, and *xingqiu*. These five kinds of pungents must not be eaten among any foods whatsoever."
If one intentionally eats [these], one commits a minor offense (light dust-offense). The *Shu* (Commentary), relying on the interpretation of the *Mingyuan*, states:

"The 'large garlic' (*dàsuàn*) is the Hu-garlic; the 'leather-garlic' (*gècōng*) is the chives; the 'orchid-garlic' (*láncōng*) is the small garlic; the 'compassionate-garlic' (*cícōng*) is the common scallion of today; and the 'xìngqú' is the *xīcài*.
The *Lù Jī’s Cāomù Chóngyú Shū* explains that the appearance of the *xīcài* resembles that of the turnip, and its flowers are purple-red in color.

"One may eat this; its appearance is similar to that of the *udumbara* flower when it arises through the cultivation of compassion. Thus, one knows that it likely exists here as well. The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:
"Mahāmati, in this way, all such pungent vegetables as onions and garlic are foul-smelling and impure;
they can obstruct the Noble Path and even obstruct the pure realms of worldly humans and devas, let alone the retributive purity of the Buddha-fields. It further says: "Mahāmati, seeking..."
Regarding the Noble Path: one should not consume alcohol, meat, leeks, scallions, garlic, or shallots—any flavors that are pungent or "fleshly.
The *Buddhottamasikhā Sūtra* states: "All sentient beings live because they eat what is sweet; they die because they eat what is toxic.
Those sentient beings who seek *samādhi* must sever the five kinds of pungent vegetables of the world. If these five pungent vegetables are eaten cooked, they arouse lust; if eaten raw..."

Consuming pungent roots increases anger in this world. Even if those who eat pungent roots can proclaim the twelve divisions of the scriptures, the celestial beings of the ten directions will loathe their foul stench and all distance themselves from them.
Various hungry ghosts, following the act of eating, lick the lips and mouths of such people;
they constantly dwell with ghosts, their merit and virtue diminish daily, and they gain no benefit. This is the cultivation of those who eat pungent roots.
The Bodhisattvas, celestial immortals, and benevolent deities of the ten directions will not come to protect them;

instead, a powerful Mara King, seeking an opportunity, will manifest in the form of a Buddha to preach the Dharma to them, reviling the prohibitions and precepts while praising lust, anger, and ignorance.

At the end of their lives, they will become followers of the Mara King, and when their demonic blessings are exhausted, they will fall into the Avīci Hell. Such are the various [teachings] of the Mahāyāna.
The sutras all state that the five pungent vegetables are obstacles to the Noble Path, and the various mantra sections universally prohibit them;
it is not merely one or two sutras that speak of their harm. The Tripitaka Master says: "Those who eat pungent vegetables fall into the great hells;

they lose even the realms of humans and devas, let alone attaining the fruits of sainthood or being reborn in a Pure Land. Yet nowadays, both monastics and laypeople fail to exercise caution, claiming they are without fault.

Furthermore, I have seen that within the vegetarian meals served at lay households and monasteries, cooks are permitted to add scallions (rǎi) at will to enhance the aroma and flavor, whether raw or cooked;
often these are used exclusively as a vegetable, which people intentionally eat and consume until their breath becomes foul and putrid.
Yet they chant the sutras and prostrate before the Buddha without the slightest hesitation. Moreover, the sutras state that when benevolent deities smell such odors, they all distance themselves.
How tragic it is that a donor should instead offer such things to the Buddha!

To provide such offerings and waste one's wealth while failing to escape hell—how much less could one hope to gain merit? Now, I judge these items to be insufficient even to aid their flavor for filling the belly.
For what reason do you so painfully crave to eat them, only to invite karmic retribution in vain? I pray you will hear this explanation and examine the Buddhist scriptures in detail.
Among all foods, none of these five pungent herbs may be eaten. To restate this in verse: The Five Pungent Herbs were taught by the Buddha;
They obstruct the Path, of this there is no doubt. In the Brahma Net Sūtra they bring minor offenses;
In the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra they damage great compassion. If even humans and devas lose [their status], How can one expect to reach the Pure Land?
Raw meat consumed increases thoughts of anger; cooked food awakens lustful desires. When the twelve divisions of the sutras are preached, celestial beings and immortals all abandon [the place];
benevolent deities do not provide protection, while evil ghosts find their advantage.
Pretas lick at the lips and mouths, and Māra manifests in the form of a Buddha; thus, one's merit and virtue are extinguished.
Karmic obstructions grow ever more pervasive; In hell, there is both bronze and iron. Bound once more by the net of saṃsāra, you indulge aimlessly in the taste of grass;
Your calamities and misfortunes are truly pitiable.
—From the *Exhortation to Donors* within the *Ritual for Recitation at the Site of the Blazing Light*.

Now, the gateways of cultivating merit and wisdom, which establish one upon the path to Bodhi, are indeed both difficult and easy. To grasp the essential meaning is easy; to lose that meaning is difficult.
It is like one who skillfully churns *amṛta*: they can obtain clarified butter (*ghṛta*); yet for one who is unskilled, even a simple drink is hard to obtain.
This is likewise so: for those who apply their minds well, a single flower or a single incense offering has merit equal to the void, and a single verse or a single phrase is the same.

If one who has accumulated the destruction of the Path and achieved what is unwholesome loses even the proximate fruits of human or celestial rebirth, how much more so the superior causes of a Bodhisattva?
A śramaṇa is called the Eye of the World; for those in the world who are blind and ignorant, he must provide guidance. Otherwise, he is not a śramaṇa.
Since the Tathāgata’s final injunction was to be without stinginess and to bestow the wealth of the Dharma upon others, and since I have honored these holy words, therefore—

I admonish you: there are donors whose households possess deep faith and devotion, inviting monks to their homes to provide food and recite scriptures, hoping thereby to increase their merit and wisdom.
Yet they exhaust themselves and waste their wealth without any virtuous ritual standards, failing to distinguish between respect and negligence, or right and wrong.
Some rely on their own wealth and status, while others act with arrogance and self-importance, even claiming that it is the gate-monks who invite them and provide for their clothing and food.
The meditation hall was treated as a place of personal favor, and those who flocked there to gaze upon it lost all sense of propriety. Lang rebuked them with clear severity.

The Dharma assembly was laid out in a convenient location, yet the gate-monks were ignorant and lacked the ability to manage the tasks; fearing they might lose their support, they preemptively avoided the labor.

Even though the donor had established proper regulations, how could the monks dare speak of them? Since the donor did not consult the gate-monks and the monks did not voice their concerns, erroneous ritual manuals have arisen from this point forward.

When the profane and ostentatious are not swept away from the hall, one sets up the Dharma seat; when the impurities of meat and pungent flavors have not been severed, one immediately invites the Sages and Worthies.
As for welcoming their images and extending reverence to them, one does not avoid sitting [in their presence], yet turns around to pay homage as if they were mere effigies.

According to the Confucian classics, "when passing by a position of superior honor, one must hasten forward. How much more so regarding the Triple Gem! Master Jingxi said: "Whenever a site for the Way is established, one ought to..."
First one must purify [the site], and only then request the image.

Regarding what people of the world say—claiming that when establishing a *bodhimaṇḍa* for the sake of seeking the Way and extinguishing obstacles, they allow ignorant children, the arrogant, and those in vulgar or naked attire to bring the image or take it away—one observes this and finds it truly pitiable.

Furthermore, it is said that even if one establishes a *bodhimaṇḍa*, if one treats the honored image with arrogance and pride, it will instead bring about the accumulation of transgressions rather than the extinction of obstacles.
Furthermore, a sutra states that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, making offerings to an image is no different from when he was in the world.

Why then do people treat it as mere wood or clay? They welcome it with great arrogance, yet show scant respect when prostrating before it; they find it strange that there is no karmic reward. Should one not reflect on this for a moment?
Moreover, Master Shibie said, "A funeral banquet or a vegetarian feast is not equal to a ritual assembly. How true these words are!
Who would be willing to listen for even a moment? To do so would be to waste wealth and effort in vain, as there is truly no karmic reward;

this is why those who are poor and destitute abound in the world while those who are wealthy and prosperous are few. For this reason, I now exhort you, O donor, to constantly associate with those of wisdom and inquire about the Buddha-dharma.
How does one cultivate profound merit and wisdom? You should humble yourself, lower your mind, and prostrate at their feet, honoring them with the utmost reverence.
Whenever the Master prepares a Dharma feast, he first goes to establish the model by solemnly sprinkling the halls and pavilions and purifying his body and mind.
He prepares and stores up fragrant incense, exotic flowers, rare fruits, and exquisite foods, and receives the visiting monks with diligent respect.

The assembly of monks reverently contemplates that the sages of the ten directions and the three periods of time are entering their home, feeling shame, trepidation, and alarm, like servants attending to a great lord or like a wife serving her husband.
Brahmins who serve the fire must follow the ritual ordinances; they must not act according to their own whims and must not shrink from diligent labor.

All matters of provision and service may be determined according to one’s own judgment. These matters number in the thousands and cannot be fully described; now I shall briefly indicate five points that can roughly be put into practice.
First, I wish to state that all members of the household attending this Dharma assembly—both elders and juniors—must be of one mind to eliminate alcohol, meat, and the five pungent herbs;
furthermore, the donor must daily prostrate with the monks and perform the confession of transgressions.

Second, when it is the turn for the monastic community’s midday meal, you must personally attend to their needs; you must not sit above the monks and act as if you were the host, indulging in idle chatter and laughter.

Third, regarding offerings before the Buddha, they must be double those made to the monastic community; treat all beings, whether ordinary or holy, with an equal mind, ensuring every detail is performed with meticulous care.

Fourth, exhaust what you cherish and give it to the Buddha and the Sangha; do not conceal the fine and use only the coarse, for this will bring about the retribution of losing one's mind in every lifetime.

Fifth, during times of urgency at the site of enlightenment, one must not employ the Sangha as servants; since they are fields of merit, how could one instead treat them like slaves? How could this be right?
Is this possible?
What I have now said will be understood by the wise; yet there may be fools who, for the sake of lay patrons (*dānapati*), find it difficult to follow and honor [this teaching].
Fearing that those gate-keeping monks, lacking discernment, might speak words of exclusion and thereby despise us, we are unable to carry out [these instructions] in their entirety.
Knowing that this text is about to be destroyed by fire, may the Triple Gem of the ten directions and all sentient beings exert their power together to protect and uphold it;
I exhort the donors to revere the Triple Gem. This is the "Text on Exhorting Donors to Respect the Triple Gem."
Petition for the Reform of Sacrifices and the Cultivation of the *Zhāi*:

I respectfully establish a *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* ritual site at the shrine of our local village, dedicated to the protection of our fields, silkworms, and people, to provide offerings of food and worship to the Buddhas and recite the Mahāyāna scriptures.
The purpose of this is to replace the annual sacrifices of meat and wine with [virtuous merit].
I have taken it upon myself to observe the fast of purity so that blessings may be equalized for the spirits, while simultaneously benefiting and bringing peace to both humans and animals.
That I specifically prepare this memorial and letter at the commencement of the rites this morning is because I reflect on the following:

the act of embracing straw to extinguish a fire arises from the extreme of ignorance, while adding fuel to stop a boiling cauldron is an act that fails to perceive the subtle signs of change—such was the folly of Tai Dian.
This is contrary to common sense and fundamentally at odds with the principles of natural law.

To metaphorically create calamity while seeking blessings, or to snatch life while praying for grace—turning the foundation of long-term disaster into a technique for longevity—is a grave error. According to the Buddhist scriptures, saving fish or feeding tigers is truly considered a method for benevolence and longevity;
yet according to the Confucian classics, slaughtering a pig while sparing a sheep is certainly not the secret formula for nourishing the spirit. At such a time as this...

In those times, when pure customs still valued simplicity and the orthodox teachings had not yet spread, people first cultivated the rituals of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius and subsequently propagated the rites of the *zheng* and *shang* sacrifices.

Reaching the Liang dynasty, the ancestral sacrifices of the entire realm were transformed into fields for fasting and purification; the teachings of the Yan family were adopted by households for ten thousand generations as a model for taking refuge [in the Triple Gem].
As humanity shifted, the world changed, customs grew thin, and the times became turbid; those who practiced goodness were isolated, while accumulated evils prevailed.

The influence of the [Former] Qin dynasty has spread throughout the masses, yet the regulations of the Liang have been lost; thus, people remain deluded by the notion that "the fragrance does not lie in the millet and grain," failing to realize that the banners and flowers are what constitute goodness.
They vie for sharpness and compete for acuity, piling up beans and adding more sacrificial vessels—how could they know that such flattery in sacrifice violates ritual propriety?

Who would say that such licentious customs ruin the rites? Even if one still opposes the regulations of Confucius, one must surely accord with the compassion of the Buddha. Now, the elders of the local districts are turning their hearts toward sincerity.

The temple sorceress cast herself down in earnest supplication, swearing an oath with the deity Xiang; she changed the sacrifices to fasts and made a solemn covenant before the Buddhas to abandon the heterodox and return to the orthodox.
Indeed, we have heard that the principle of Heaven and Earth is upright observation, and the virtue of the sun and moon is upright illumination.

When Heaven and Earth are in harmony, the myriad things flourish; when the sun and moon revolve, the four seasons accord with their proper measures. Once the two polarities are measured, all considerations find their place.
One may exhaustively investigate the spirits and things that govern the hidden realm, and preside over human relations in the manifest world.

When the hearts of the divine and the human interact, the Way between the hidden and the manifest is thereby fully realized. If humans do not revere the spirits, upon what could the source of blessings and calamities rest?

If the hidden realm is not in harmony with the manifest, then the rites of *di* and *chang* sacrifices would be performed in vain. Since the spirit borrows human vitality and the spirit must follow human wishes, people now take refuge in the Buddha.
May the spirits likewise return to the Buddha; if the Buddha delivers others, may the spirits likewise deliver me.

The Buddha’s compassion, flowing from ten thousand virtues, is no different from the boundless mercy of the Ten Directions. Like the bright sun moving through the great void, it illuminates both valleys and mountain peaks;
like torrential rain falling upon the vast fields, it moistens both grasses and trees alike. Displaying his supernatural powers, he strikes fear into the wicked with a clap of thunder.

In vain they raise the sounds of the Dharma; the winds of the True Teaching rush forth. The Four Kings receive their mandates upon the lecture seat, and the Eight Classes of Beings distribute their edicts from among the rows.
Thus, transformation reaches the limits of the six voids, and grace encompasses the myriad species.

Therefore, even fierce bandits bow their heads before the golden images in the heavenly shrines, and young children prostrate themselves before the gods and spirits in the vast wilderness. We humans and devas alike pay homage!

Together we celebrate having heard these remaining tones; our local kin share this same affinity as we encounter this Age of the Image. We realize that the path of birth and death is long and, at its end, where can one find refuge?
We awaken to the suffering of being smeared with mud and scorched in fire—a plight vast and eternal from which there is no return.

Now, wishing to refine the beautiful and supplement the ugly, to reform the past and cultivate the future, we shall sweep and cleanse the divine shrine and solemnize the Buddha’s assembly, transforming the short dance into the form of majestic deportment.
The long songs were transformed into the sounds of the Vaipulya sutras; the ritual vessels were filled to capacity with pure offerings, and the white sacrificial foods were set out.

Thorny branches were removed and the seeds of the *īraṇa* were uprooted; weeds were burned away and the roots of the *campaka* were planted. The blood of beasts no longer flowed in the mountain streams and ravines, and the crows and owls perched upon the trees ceased their clamor.
Pigs and sheep attained their natural state, and fish and birds rejoiced in heaven; the village and its surroundings were suddenly transformed, becoming entirely identical to a Pure Land.
I humbly entreat the Buddhas of the ten directions to arrive together with the eight classes of beings, and the Sangha of the ten stages to descend alongside those of the three vehicles.
May you take pity upon me, a child who has cast myself into the flames, and grant the grace of rescuing me from suffering. First I repent for the three miserable realms;

next I pray for the five blessings. Looking upward, I reflect upon the solemn shrines, the secret rulers, the numinous precincts, and the dark officials—those deities who formerly shared in the sacrificial offerings, now [present].

May those who have temporarily turned back from the holy fast of the communal reform, you of noble character, examine these virtuous words. Daring to rely upon the Buddhist scriptures, I pray that your divine ears will listen.

Since the forms of the nine abodes have not yet been shed, the principles of the three miserable realms must remain unfailing. If one slaughters livestock for the sake of a deity, how can that deity escape the retribution of the future?
Because of the Buddha, one renounces the five pungent roots; because of the Buddha, one opens the gate of repentance for past transgressions. Now that awakening has been attained—

Let no past transgressions give rise to future regret; for a mere moment, cups, platters, meats, and wine are enjoyed as offerings, yet thereafter form and shadow become enemies, entangled through vast kalpas.
Households are like silkworms worrying over public levies, and fields serve as provisions for grain. We pray only for the grace of hidden protection; who would fear the affairs of the dark pass?
When we die, there is nowhere to go; there is no spirit that is not honored. Thus, the three sacrificial objects are brought forth to swear this oath.

In different locations they offer sacrifices; some are boiled, some are flayed, some are roasted, and some are burned. The stench of the village spreads for miles, and the cries of agony from the fields reach one after another.

By the time they arrive at the sacrificial altar before the honored spirits, there is none who does not simultaneously cherish their children and protect their wives—who would realize that their fear of death and greed for life are no different from others?
Who would be willing to awaken to the truth that killing others to sustain oneself is no different from treating humans as mere beasts?

When a sharp blade is drawn and held over one's head, how could one not cry out for the time when one recognized its master? When holding a ritual vessel to the mouth, one does not think of returning home in the evening to raise it as if it were a son;
yet when it is killed, its feathers are torn and its horns shattered—yet even so, it still understands the meaning of the ring in its mouth to repay its master.

How can it be that there are none who, like the "tapping of the sword-hilt" (the hungry cat), harbor resentment and beg the Three Jewels for assistance to uplift those already fallen, causing them all to attain liberation?

Having been liberated from the constraints of the hundred deities and severed from the bonds that remain unharmed, I shall forever attain the state of carefree wandering (*vīta-rāga*). Having already purified my mind through repentance, I hope to extinguish my transgressions.
By day, I am moved by the illumination of the sun, reaching the karmic nature of King Daśaratha;

by night, I am reached by the sound of the golden drum, forever uprooting the root of doubt like that of the Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa. I now look upward to dedicate these merits entirely to the spirits of the temple, so that they may be granted sovereign power.

In the realm of supernormal powers, you preserve your leisurely dwelling in the abode of immortals; formerly, when you partook of the fine fish and fragrant wine, you still bestowed blessings in abundance.
Now, having been moistened by the sweet dew and the clarified butter, you further grant us auspicious peace and harmony. With a single-minded heart, you bestow boundless protection;

may the ten rains and five winds ensure a bountiful harvest for the coming year. As for our provision of offerings to the Sangha and the Buddhas, we dare vow to repay your kindness throughout all of existence.
In autumn, we still pray for silkworms to flourish and fields to abound, so that our livelihoods may expand within our bags and satchels.

May those upon our plains and slopes all live to a full hundred years; may infants and children be nurtured with the five blessings. May wives be virtuous, sons filial, elder brothers compliant, and younger brothers respectful.

May universal love extend to kin and benevolence toward others, so that one may employ this to honor virtue. May the Sage Song dynasty remain ever peaceful today, and may the Benevolent Ruler endure forever.

May the devas, nāgas, and spirits protect the state and the Dharma, so that all sentient beings within the realm of phenomena may be freed from suffering and attain happiness. Yet, among them, there are those who, not understanding the benefits or harms involved, recklessly give rise to slander and destruction, claiming that sacrifices performed by laypeople— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.)
Some previously claimed that fasting and precept-keeping cannot save one in times of urgency;

seeing others practice vegetarianism and recite the Buddha’s name, they thought, "I shall simply maintain my mind," believing that when the causes and conditions of good and evil arise in future lives, who else will receive the karmic retribution? Consequently, those whose roots of goodness were not yet deep became confused and disturbed by these views, causing many to retreat from their initial resolve.
Now, in order to sever such doubts, I shall cite scriptural evidence and compose verses for easy memorization and retention, following [the teachings].
These are true words; do not believe in heterodox doctrines. However, because people of the world harbor doubts, I shall now briefly record ten verses from the *Anantamukha-sādhaka*.
The first doubt concerns whether ghosts exist or not, and whether they can bring about calamity or fortune.
The commentary states: The Sūtras speak of the six realms of existence, and spirits occupy one of them; why then doubt that there are no spirits?

The *Āgama* Sūtras say that all dwellings—houses, streets, lanes, alleys, slaughterhouses, marketplaces, as well as mountains and burial mounds—are inhabited by spirits and deities, yet they cannot benefit or harm humans.
The *Upamā-sūtra* says that the spirits and deities of the world do not...
They can neither bring life to people nor kill them, nor can they cause people to become wealthy or poor;

they merely manifest as strange spirits (*graha*) according to the decline and inferiority of individuals, hoping for offerings and sacrifices. If one seeks blessings from them, they will certainly not be obtained.
The worldly, unaware of this, are pointlessly deceived; some even kill living beings and commit evil deeds. A verse says: [Verse follows]

Ghosts and spirits exist everywhere, deceiving and deluding the people of the world; making offerings to ghosts brings no merit at all, only increasing the causes for karmic retribution through killing.
Second Doubt: We see with our own eyes that when worldly people fall ill, they obtain peace and security by performing sacrifices; how can you say there is no merit?
The commentary states: Among worldly people, poverty, illness, misfortune, and fortune all pertain to cause and effect;

they cannot be produced by ghosts. That ghosts bring about calamity is generally summoned through false faith and obtained through sycophantic seeking. As the *Vādanyāya* (Discourse on Distinguishing Right from Wrong) says: "Old ghosts instruct new ghosts to stir up怪异 (strange anomalies) and seek food.
When they first go to two households, they turn the millstones and grind upon the pestles. Those households worship the Buddha and do not believe [in ghosts]."
This is strange: everyone says that benevolent deities assisted me, yet all day long I pounded and ground several *hu* of rice and wheat and could not eat a single grain.

Later, I entered the home of a family with heterodox beliefs and ordered a white dog to walk through the air; the family was greatly amazed, killed the dog, and prepared a feast for me, whereby I finally became full.
You should know that believing in the Buddha does not require belief in such wonders; even if you were to see them—
If you simply focus exclusively on reciting the Buddha’s name, such calamities will naturally subside. The verse says:

With right faith, devas and dragons provide protection; How could malevolent spirits prevail? Know only that by constantly reciting the Buddha’s name, Calamities and strange portents will naturally be consumed away.
Third, there is doubt as to whether those whose family members have died can obtain food through ancestral offerings or not.
The commentary states: If one falls among the hungry ghosts (*preta*), one may sometimes obtain food at the time of an offering;

however, for those ghosts who dwell in the "Flaming Mouth" (*yankou*) hell, even if an offering is made, they cannot obtain food. The *Āgama* Sūtra says: "If one performs almsgiving and offerings for the sake of the deceased..."
If one dies and enters among the hungry ghosts (*preta*), they may obtain food; if born in other realms, they will certainly not obtain it.
Among the myriad species of the six destinies, the retributions received differ vastly. When parents die, how could they all necessarily become ghosts?
That worldly people do not recognize this and unilaterally perform sacrifices is utterly irrational. The verse says:

When a person dies, they follow their prior karma, ascending or sinking through the six realms in various ways. How can it be that performing sacrifices alone is said to be the folly of worldly people?

(The Fourth Doubt: The Extensive Nature of Sacrificial Rites) The methods of sacrifice are extensively detailed in the Ritual Classics (*Lijing*). The Son of Heaven has seven ancestral temples, while the feudal lords have five. Great...
Now, from the high ministers down to the common people, all alike perform sacrifices at the Round Mound and the Square Pond to worship the spirits of heaven and earth;
this is the constant ordinance of the state. How can you urge them to cease these sacrifices? It would cause great injury to the national customs.

according to the Buddhist sutras, one values only compassion. Killing results in retribution within the three miserable realms (*trāya*), whereas compassion results in the perfection of the ten thousand virtues.
By transforming evil with good and leading the shallow toward the profound, the Buddha delivers all sentient beings without exception.
Now that you people have already placed faith in Buddhism, you must cultivate the compassion of the Buddha and must no longer kill sentient beings while claiming to be disciples of the Buddha;

how much more so when, according to common worldly custom, not only do you sacrifice to your ancestors, but there is no deity to whom you do not pay homage—indeed, these are called licentious sacrifices where true virtue is not cultivated and one attends only to the taking of life.
This is a matter of profound lamentation that cannot be fully exhausted by brief discussion. Thus, in the past, Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty...
The Emperor issued an edict throughout the realm to abolish sacrifices and cease killing; this was surely in accordance with the Buddhist teachings, not only today.
Now that there is the merit of the fast, it is precisely the time to compete in cultivation; this will sufficiently benefit both the living and the deceased, and also spare the lives of creatures.
Why labor under the burden of rigidly adhering to sacrificial rites? The verse says: [Verse omitted as per instructions]

Slaughtering oxen out of shame regarding the *yue* sacrifice—though millet and grain are not inherently fragrant; chanting with purity is true brilliance and virtue, so why labor over adhering to the ritual classics?

On the night he was to provide a vegetarian feast (*zhāi*), Zhang Ying dreamed that a divine being reproached him for not having prepared the offerings with early purity.

Using skillful means, he uttered the bleat of a sheep and died.

when the local people brought oxen and wine as offerings, the magistrate tied the ox to a pillar, removed the Buddhist images, and arranged couches and seats [in their place].

He died while crying out in distress. Gao Wei of Jiangling followed me into the Qi state for several years;
later, while fishing in the marshes of Youzhou, he fell ill, and every time he saw a school of fish biting him, he would die. Furthermore, there was a man in the Song dynasty... [text continues]
Anju’s parents were believers in the teachings of Śākyamuni; they performed fasts and recitations morning and evening. An elder brother of theirs served a deity whose image filled the house.

Regarding the sacrifice of living beings, it would be better to cut one's own four limbs than to kill a life;

Turning away from the heterodox, one gives rise to right faith; From stinking grass, sandalwood emerges. When encountering difficulties, one must remain steadfast;

The Explanation states: Simply by single-mindedly reciting the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva every day, all disasters, all illnesses, imprisonment, bandits and thieves, water, fire, wind, thunder and lightning, tigers, wolves, venomous snakes, insects, and malevolent spells will [be overcome].

None can cause them harm. As stated in the *Avalokiteśvara-bodhisattva-nāma-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, the Buddha commanded all the great devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and all powerful divine generals to protect day and night those who uphold the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva;

An Inscription on a Wilderness Shrine:

The ignorant common folk undertake matters without fail being perverse; they abandon benevolence and pursue slaughter, hoping thereby to prolong their lives. They dilute virtue with licentious sacrifices, hoping thereby to secure blessings for themselves.
Such is the custom of these mountain and sea regions—a perversion of the Way. By the roadside trees grow lush and tall.
Others, suspecting him of possessing divine power, would immediately cut paper to present as an offering at the mountain foot;
others, measuring his spiritual efficacy, would arrange beans to sacrifice at the riverbank.

Those within the village who could speak revered him as a shaman, and the shaman then let loose his ignorance, first bowing before the water and trees to formally name and substantiate the affairs of the dwelling and its physical form.
I suspect that because the threads [of order] have no end, he fell ill and grew anxious over the onset of drought and floods, returning the calamity to this [sacrifice].
It began with a single room, then gradually spread to a hundred rooms; it began with small offerings, which did not stop until there were great sacrifices.
In some years, these were performed three or four times. How could such a poor and destitute man be performing the rites for the spirits? Alas! The family has no means of sustaining itself.
If disaster arises from non-spiritual causes, am I unable to save you? Furthermore, when a tree first grows, why does it not become divine of its own accord, waiting for man to make it divine?

When water first flows, why does it not become numinous of its own accord, waiting for man to make it numinous? Once a spirit has already accepted its offerings of blood, why not honor it with jade and silk?
If it can transform paper into wealth, why not transform earth into food? What food would it eat?
That humans are esteemed while wealth is held cheap is the height of perversion of the natural order—stop, stop!
I have heard it said: "In a family that accumulates goodness, there will surely be an abundance of blessings; in a family that accumulates evil, there will surely be an abundance of calamity.

Is the spirit far away? It resides only where the mind carries it. Is the numinous power far away? It exists only where the person is present. Yet people compete with each other over water and trees as if they were fools.

Furthermore, in the "Chapter on Discerning Delusions Regarding the Three Robes," it is recorded that the Buddha ordained that Dharma robes consist of only three types: first, the *antaravāsaka*; second, the *uttarāsaṅga*; and third, the *saṃghāṭī*.
Kāli! These three dharma-robes are definitively the attire of those who have left the household life; they are not worn by laypeople. The *Saṃghīti* states:
"The three robes are the insignia of the noble śramaṇas, not something for worldly persons. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Because the holy disciples of the Buddha abide in the Middle Way, they wear the three robes. The non-Buddhists go naked and lack shame, while white-robed [laypeople] are full of greed."
The *Saṃyukta Āgama* further records that those who cultivate the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*) do so by shaving their hair, donning the three dharma robes, and leaving the household life.
Based on this, it is certain that one does not wear secular clothing.

As for the claim that the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* mentions the wearing [of robes] by laypeople, when people see that sūtra’s extensive listing of kings, ministers, monastics, and laity all being able to receive the precepts, they conclude that one should teach [the recipient] to wear the *kāṣāya* upon their body.

The mention of the *sa* (sāṭī) and other garments leads those among men and women who have received the Bodhisattva precepts to wear the seven-strip robe (*saptaka-kaṣāya*). Upon examining the text of that sūtra, however, it does not seem to be the case that this was intended for all.

The term *kāṣāya* (袈裟) is correctly translated as "dyed" (*rañjita*) or alternatively as "reclining gear" (*śayanāsana*). According to the translation "dyed," it serves as a general regulation for both monastics and laypeople;

yet, when receiving the precepts, one must wear colors that have been discolored (*khaṇḍa-varṇa*). This is because there is a fear that if the dyeing were identical to that of ordinary, brilliant colors, it would contravene the established regulations of the Dharma.
It is then stated that, according to the teachings, the robes worn on the body should all be dyed in a discolored hue (*kāṣāya*).

Alternatively, because certain local customs cannot be entirely regulated, a renunciant bodhisattva must necessarily dye their robes to a discolored hue. Furthermore, the text states: "A bhikṣu should differ from those who wear secular clothing.

When has he ever followed the common practice of wearing the seven-strip robe (*saptaka-cīvara*)? Or when has he [worn] what is translated as a bedding cloth (*śayanāsana*)? Nanshan says that the three robes (*tricīvara*) constitute the whole.
The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states that wearing the nine-striped, seven-striped, or five-striped *kāṣāya* is precisely its textual description.
If this is so, what prevents the term *kāṣāya* from referring specifically to the robes of those who have left the household life? Furthermore, the text itself says:

"A *bhikṣu* should always wear clothing different from that of the laity. Both the commentaries of Tiantai and Master Zang interpret this according to the meaning of "dyeing and destroying" (the natural color).
There is no teaching regarding "lay three-robes" (*sāṃghāṭī*);

although within the Vaipulya sutras it is permitted to wear the three robes when entering the *maṇḍala* for lay repentance, they must be single-seamed (*dān-fèng*, pronounced level tone) and not double-stitched (*què-cì*, with *cì* pronounced *qī jí*). The Buddha said: "These three robes are:
first, the single-seamed; second, the lay garment. Master Jingxi said: "If they were double-stitched, they would be..."

The robes worn by the Great Sangha are those they receive and maintain; therefore, these robes must be made separately. It is deeply improper for there to be instances in the world where one borrows the robes of an ordained monk.
Thus we know that although the three robes exist, they are not themselves the attire of the renunciant (as stated in the *Fuxingji*).

If one has faith in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, and if it has already been permitted to wear the *Vaipulya* [robes], why then must they be sewn single-layered? Even according to the *Āgamas*, the Buddha ordered them to take the *Aṃśuka* [robe].

The account of Nandayudrāṅga giving the *saṃghāṭī* robe to the daughter of Vāsiṣṭha, such that it was equal [in size], originated from the Sage’s intention to respond momentarily to a specific occasion.
After his parinirvāṇa, ordinary beings must follow the established regulations. All the precepts were proclaimed again in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* as his final words;

these alone constitute the definitive standard. While the three robes are permitted for laypeople, there is no textual evidence for this in that sūtra. Others may claim it wards off calamities or avoids misfortune.
It is permitted to grant small pieces, such as those temporarily hung by a courtesan upon a hunter’s borrowed cloak;

it is said that with four inches one’s food and drink are satisfied, and by hanging a single piece, the rākṣasa does not devour one. This clearly demonstrates the utility of the three robes (*tricīvara*), rather than permitting their possession by the four classes of laypeople.
Even those who have left the household life to dwell in seclusion and distance themselves from evil are still ignorant of the rules for wearing these robes while amidst the secular world.

In this world of such clamor and confusion, who truly knows the protocols for honoring the Dharma? Nanshan said: "If one’s use [of requisites] is according to the proper method, no transgression will arise;

but if one accepts them in a manner contrary to the rules, one will surely fall into deep guilt. Throughout one's life, there will be no clothing to cover the body, and at death, one will personally bear the retribution of the Sages.
What need is there to worry about a share in the evil realms? Reflecting on these words, I realize I am sitting amidst profound faults and must endure [the consequences].

To unjustly and erroneously implicate laypeople further incurs transgression and delusion; one cannot remain silent before seeing so many monastics and laypeople vying to wear *luozis* (sleeveless vests), a practice whose origins are long-standing and whose proliferation is now imminent.
Furthermore, regarding the three robes (*tricīvara*) and five rags (*pañcakaṣāya*), these are permitted by two distinct codes of discipline.
From what scripture does the name or form of the *luozǐ* originate? If one were to take fragments of the three robes and transform them into this garment, it would be a violation for a *bhikṣu*.

When robes are damaged, they should simply be mended so that their formal acceptance and possession (*parigraha*) are not lost; how can one allow them to be worn in such a tattered state under another name?
How is this any different from a bhikṣu who has lost his robes after being robbed?

Some claim it is permissible to hang them up temporarily while performing work within the monastery, but if that is the case, why not wear the *antarvāsa* (inner robe), which is specifically a garment for use within the monastery? As for lay disciples...

If one seeks to avoid calamities and misfortunes, one should not always wear a mere fragment of the *kāṣāya*. If it were permitted to wear it constantly, why would one not permit the full set of three robes (*tricīvara*) instead of merely a single fragment?
Master Nanshan cites the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, which records that a dragon was spared from the peril of the *garuḍa* by wearing the *kāṣāya*; he then remarks:

"If one does not comply with the teachings, the *kāṣāya* worn upon them will lack power. If even [wearing] the *kāṣāya* in violation of the teachings is said to be powerless, how much more so is this the case for a mere fragment?
How much more so now, when *luozis* (netted bags) are openly manufactured, newly cut and dyed; both in name and substance, they are entirely contrary to the Dharma.

Examining this, one knows that those who wear them incur transgression and lack merit. I have here briefly recorded three faults of violating the teachings, hoping that upon reading them, you will pardon no offense, however great, and surely reform toward goodness.
First, the name and substance of the *luozis* are not recorded anywhere in the regulations.

First, regarding the permission for the two teachings, since everything therein is non-existent and one lacks the five merits, yet one indiscriminately participates in the three base classes, the responsibility for violating the teachings and the karmic retribution in the afterlife are not false.

Second, regarding the prohibition against permitting the two teachings: only the Buddha alone [is authorized]; from the Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas downward, they merely transmit what was taught and do not compose their own works.
Now that you have composed your own "net-pattern" (luòzǐ), O Benevolent One, are you then the Buddha? Third, you follow the ranks of the external paths.

Regarding those who are not followers of the Buddha, Nanshan said that sewing strips of various colored threads onto one's robes is the dharma of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), constituting a *sthalāñchana* (a sectarian mark).
How much more so for creating robes that violate the Dharma; this is utterly contrary to the original regulations. If these are not the ranks of the non-Buddhists, then who are they?
I hope that practitioners of the Mahāyāna from the four quarters will read this text and seek its meaning, and not [follow such practices].

To guard one’s own feelings while carrying hemp and discarding gold is truly not the way of the wise. To reform abuses and follow what is correct is how the enlightened person should understand the unsurpassed Buddha-vehicle.
Regarding the method for upholding and transmitting the understanding that there is no distinction between the secular and the monastic, it truly lies in the Vinaya;

the Nirvana Sutra supports the Vinaya by discussing the eternal, and its very essence resides herein. If the disciplinary model is destroyed, who will transmit the Dharma? How could one be born as a human being and yet fail to uphold it?
"To protect one's eyes and sever the constant thread of life—is this not the way of a *caṇḍāla*? In the past, Dharma Master Jing’ai encountered the tyranny of Emperor Wu of the Zhou dynasty.
Remorseful that he could not protect the Dharma, he lamented, 'What is the use of being a renunciant?

Thereupon, he sat upon a rock, took up a blade, carved the flesh from his entire body, drew out his intestines to hang from a tree, and finally, cupping his heart in his hands, passed away. Alas! Such was the manner in which the sages of antiquity protected the Dharma."

Since we have studied this yet remain unable to master it, we should strictly observe the established regulations so as not to cause damage or ruin that would bring calamity upon ourselves and others.
